policy_title: Infection Prevention and Control Practices in Clinical Areas
purpose:
This document sets out how {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} prevents the transmission of infection to patients, staff, visitors and the wider community during the delivery of care in clinical areas. It translates the infection prevention and control programme of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} into working instructions covering standard precautions, hand hygiene, transmission-based precautions, safe injection and infusion practice, protection of staff before and after occupational exposure, and the controlled use of antimicrobial agents.

The intent is threefold: to make the expected behaviour unambiguous for every person who works in or enters a clinical area; to reduce healthcare-associated infection and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance within {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}; and to generate the records that demonstrate the programme is genuinely operating in practice rather than existing only on paper.
scope:
This policy applies across every clinical and clinical-support area of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, including inpatient wards, intensive and high-dependency areas, operation theatres and procedure rooms, the labour room, emergency and casualty, outpatient consulting and treatment rooms, dialysis, day-care, imaging and interventional suites, laboratory specimen-handling areas, central sterile supply, and pharmacy medication-preparation areas — in short, anywhere invasive procedures, injections or infusions are performed or patients receive direct care.

It applies to all doctors including visiting and honorary consultants, nurses, technicians, therapists, pharmacists, housekeeping and sanitation staff, dietary staff, security staff, biomedical and maintenance personnel, students and trainees on clinical attachment, and contracted or outsourced personnel working within these areas. The provisions on hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene and compliance with precaution signage extend to patients, attendants and visitors.

The provisions on staff immunisation and on management of occupational exposure apply to every person engaged by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, whether directly employed or contracted, who may come into contact with blood, body fluids, biomedical waste or food. The sections on antimicrobial usage and antibiotic stewardship apply to every prescriber at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} and to the hospital pharmacy.
policy_statement:
{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} treats infection prevention and control as a condition of practising in a clinical area, not as an additional task that competes with clinical work.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} applies standard precautions to every patient during every episode of care, at all times, without reference to the patient's diagnosis, presumed risk or infection status. Where an agent is known or suspected that standard precautions alone will not contain, transmission-based precautions are applied in addition — contact, droplet or airborne as the route of transmission requires, and in combination where more than one route applies.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} adopts the World Health Organization's five moments and its published handrub and handwash techniques as the hospital standard, provides the facilities and consumables that make compliance physically possible at the point of care, and measures compliance by direct observation so that the figure reported is an observed one.

Every injection and infusion at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is prepared and given aseptically on the principle of one needle, one syringe, one patient, one time. Sharps are disposed of by the person who used them, at the point of use, into a puncture-proof container. Blood and body fluid spills are contained and decontaminated immediately by the staff of the area in which they occur. Biomedical waste is segregated at the point of generation into the colour-coded streams required by the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} protects its own staff as well as its patients. Vaccination against hepatitis B is offered to everyone with potential exposure to blood or body fluids, at no cost to the individual and before exposure rather than after it, and occupational exposures are managed as time-critical events under a defined post-exposure protocol.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} maintains a written antimicrobial usage policy that is approved, dated, version-controlled, available in every clinical area and built on the hospital's own antibiogram. Prescribing is monitored against that policy, restricted agents are dispensed only against a recorded authorisation, and consumption and resistance trends are reviewed by the Infection Control Committee. Where {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} operates an antibiotic stewardship programme, it is run against the recognised core elements of hospital stewardship and produces measurable outcome data. Surveillance of healthcare-associated infection is conducted using standard published case definitions, so that the effect of these practices is measured rather than assumed.

Every member of staff at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is individually responsible for compliance with this policy and is empowered to stop and to challenge an unsafe practice, irrespective of the seniority of the person performing it, without fear of adverse consequence. Reporting a breach, a sharps injury, a spill or a near miss is treated as a system-improvement input; the response is directed at correcting the cause rather than penalising the individual, except in cases of wilful or repeated disregard.
procedure_steps:
1. Governance and ownership of the programme

The Infection Control Committee (ICC) of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} owns this policy and is accountable for the programme described in it. An Infection Control Nurse (ICN) or equivalent designated officer runs it day to day. The ICC constitution, chairperson, member roles, quorum and meeting frequency are recorded separately in the committee terms of reference — [Hospital to define]. Every clinical area of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} nominates a link nurse or link person who acts as the local point of contact for infection control matters and who escalates observed breaches without waiting for a scheduled meeting.

3. Hand hygiene — the five moments at which hands must be cleaned

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} follows the World Health Organization's "My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" model. Hands are cleaned:

Moment 1 — Before touching a patient. Performed on moving from the general healthcare area into the patient zone, before any contact. This protects the patient from organisms carried on the hands of staff.

Moment 2 — Before a clean or aseptic procedure. Performed immediately before touching a critical site carrying infection risk — for example before inserting or accessing a vascular device or urinary catheter, before wound care, before preparing an injection, and before handling invasive equipment. This protects the patient from organisms, including the patient's own, entering the body.

Moment 3 — After a body fluid exposure risk. Performed immediately after any actual or potential exposure to blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes or non-intact skin, and immediately after removing gloves. This protects the member of staff and the environment from the patient's organisms.

Moment 4 — After touching a patient. Performed on leaving the patient zone, after contact with the patient and before touching anything in the general healthcare area.

Moment 5 — After touching the patient's surroundings. Performed after touching any object or surface within the patient zone — bed rails, bedside locker, infusion pump, monitor, linen — even where the patient was not touched at all.

Moments 1 and 2 are performed before the action; Moments 3, 4 and 5 are performed after it. Where two moments coincide, a single hand hygiene action satisfies both.

4. Choosing between alcohol-based handrub and soap and water

Alcohol-based handrub is the routine method at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} for all five moments when hands are not visibly soiled, because it acts faster, is better tolerated by the skin and can be sited at the point of care.

Hands are washed with soap and running water instead of using handrub when:
- hands are visibly dirty or visibly soiled with blood or other body fluid;
- hands feel sticky after repeated handrub applications;
- there has been exposure to, or care of a patient with, a spore-forming organism such as Clostridioides difficile, where alcohol is not reliably effective; and
- before eating and after using the toilet.

Handrub and soap-and-water are not applied one immediately after the other as a routine, since this offers no additional benefit and damages the skin.

5. Technique — alcohol-based handrub, 20 to 30 seconds

The whole action takes 20 to 30 seconds. Rings, wrist watches and bracelets are removed first, and sleeves are kept above the elbow.

Apply a palmful of handrub into a cupped hand — enough to wet all surfaces of both hands — then rub through the following six movements, each repeated at least five times:

(1) Palm against palm.
(2) Right palm over the back of the left hand with the fingers interlaced, then left palm over the back of the right hand.
(3) Palm against palm with the fingers interlaced, cleaning the finger webs.
(4) Backs of the fingers against the opposing palm with the fingers interlocked.
(5) The left thumb clasped in the right palm and rubbed with a rotating movement, then the right thumb in the left palm.
(6) The clasped fingertips of the right hand rubbed in a rotating, backwards-and-forwards movement against the left palm, then the fingertips of the left hand in the right palm.

Rub until the hands are completely dry. The hands are safe only once dry — the alcohol must be allowed to evaporate and must not be wiped, fanned or dried on clothing. Gloves are never put on over wet hands.

6. Technique — soap and running water, 40 to 60 seconds

The whole action takes 40 to 60 seconds.

Wet the hands with water. Apply enough soap to cover every surface of both hands. Work through the same six rubbing movements set out in step 5, in the same order and for the same number of repetitions. Rinse the hands thoroughly with water. Dry them completely with a single-use towel. Use that same towel to turn off the tap, then discard it — hands are not re-contaminated on a tap handle that was touched with dirty hands. Where the basin has a hands-free tap, this last step is unnecessary.

Hot water is not used, as it increases the risk of dermatitis without improving decontamination. Bar soap in an open dish is not used anywhere in {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}; liquid soap is supplied in wall-mounted dispensers that are not topped up on to a partly used refill.

7. Conditions that make correct hand hygiene possible

Staff of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} working in clinical areas keep fingernails short, clean and free of nail polish, gel and artificial nails. Hand and wrist jewellery is not worn during clinical care; a plain band, where cultural or personal circumstances make removal unacceptable, is moved and the skin beneath it cleaned during every hand hygiene action.

Cuts and abrasions on the hands are covered with a waterproof dressing before duty. Staff with dermatitis, cracked skin or an open lesion on the hands report to the ICN, who assesses fitness for direct patient contact. Because damaged skin carries higher organism counts and makes staff avoid hand hygiene, {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} provides hand moisturiser compatible with the handrub in use and encourages its regular application.

8. Hand hygiene facilities, taps and consumables

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} places alcohol-based handrub within arm's reach of the point of care — at the entry to each bed space, on each medication and procedure trolley, at ward entry and exit points, and at the entrance to every intensive care and procedure area — so that no member of staff has to leave the patient zone to perform hand hygiene.

Handwash basins in patient care areas are of adequate size and depth to contain splashing during handwashing, and are provided with running water, liquid soap in a wall-mounted dispenser, and single-use towels or tissue for drying. Hands-free taps — elbow, foot, knee or sensor operated — are preferred at all clinical handwash basins, because a hand-operated tap re-contaminates hands that have just been washed.

In the operation theatre scrub area, hands-free taps are mandatory: taps must be elbow, foot or sensor operated, without exception. Any OT scrub basin at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} still fitted with a hand-operated tap is converted, and until conversion is complete the basin is not used for surgical scrubbing.

Housekeeping checks every dispenser at the start of each shift and refills empty units immediately. Refill and dispenser-fault checks are logged; the log is reviewed by the ICN at a frequency of [Hospital to define]. Dispensers found empty on more than one check are treated as an infection control incident and reported to the ICC, not simply refilled.

The WHO handrub and handwash technique diagrams and the 5 Moments diagram are displayed above every basin and beside every handrub dispenser throughout {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, in English and in the local language.

9. Monitoring hand hygiene compliance

The ICN or a trained and validated observer conducts direct-observation audits in each clinical area of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}. Observation is open — staff are told that hand hygiene is being observed — and each session runs for approximately 20 minutes (plus or minus 10 minutes) so the observer can record accurately.

The observer counts opportunities (each occurrence of one or more of the five moments) and records whether a hand hygiene action was performed at each. Compliance is calculated as:

Compliance (%) = (number of hand hygiene actions performed ÷ total number of opportunities observed) × 100

Results are calculated separately by professional category (doctors, nurses, technicians, housekeeping) and by clinical area, because a single hospital-wide figure conceals where the problem sits. Audit frequency and the compliance target adopted by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} are [Hospital to define].

Results are fed back to the audited area within [Hospital to define] of the observation, displayed on the ward notice board, and tabled at the ICC. Where an area falls below target, the ICC records a named corrective action with an owner and a due date, and re-audits that area to confirm whether the action worked. Consumption of handrub per 1,000 patient-days is tracked from stores issue data as a supporting indicator, since direct observation alone can be influenced by the presence of the observer.

10. Selecting personal protective equipment

Staff of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} select PPE by anticipating the exposure the task will produce, not by the label attached to the patient.

- Gloves: for anticipated contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or contaminated items.
- Gown or plastic apron: where clothing or exposed skin is likely to be contaminated or splashed.
- Surgical mask: where splashing or spraying towards the face is possible, and for droplet precautions.
- Particulate respirator (N95 or equivalent): for airborne precautions and for aerosol-generating procedures.
- Eye protection — goggles or a face shield: where splashing towards the eyes is possible.

PPE is put on before entering the patient zone and removed before leaving it. It is not worn from one patient to the next, is not worn in corridors, staff rooms, nursing stations or dining areas, and is not washed, disinfected or re-used where it is single-use.

11. Sequence for putting on PPE (donning)

PPE is put on in this order, outside the patient room or immediately inside the doorway:

(1) Perform hand hygiene.
(2) Gown — cover the torso from neck to knees and the arms to the wrists, wrap it around the back, and fasten at the neck and waist.
(3) Mask or respirator — secure the ties or elastics at the middle of the head and at the neck, mould the flexible band over the bridge of the nose, and check that it sits close to the face and below the chin. A respirator additionally requires a user seal check on every occasion.
(4) Goggles or face shield — position over the eyes and face and adjust to fit.
(5) Gloves — pull on last and extend them over the cuff of the gown so no wrist skin is exposed.

12. Sequence for removing PPE (doffing)

Doffing is where self-contamination happens, so it is performed slowly and deliberately. Except for the mask or respirator, PPE is removed at the doorway or in the anteroom, before leaving the patient room; the mask or respirator is removed after leaving the room and closing the door.

(1) Gloves — the outside is contaminated. Grasp the outside of one glove near the wrist with the other gloved hand and peel it off, turning it inside out, and hold it in the still-gloved hand. Slide the ungloved fingers under the wrist of the remaining glove and peel it off over the first glove. Discard into the correct waste container.
(2) Goggles or face shield — the outside is contaminated. Handle only the headband or ear pieces, lift away from the face, and discard or place in the designated container for reprocessing.
(3) Gown — the front and sleeves are contaminated. Unfasten the ties, pull the gown away from the neck and shoulders touching only the inside, turn it inside out as it comes off, roll it into a bundle and discard.
(4) Leave the room and close the door.
(5) Mask or respirator — the front is contaminated and is never touched. Grasp the lower tie or elastic first, then the upper one, lift the item away from the face and discard.
(6) Perform hand hygiene.

Hand hygiene is performed immediately at any point during doffing at which the hands are thought to have been contaminated, without waiting until the end of the sequence.

13. Gloves — specific rules

Gloves supplement hand hygiene; they never replace it. Hand hygiene is performed both before putting gloves on and immediately after taking them off, because gloves develop unseen defects and hands are contaminated during removal.

Gloves are changed between patients without exception. They are also changed between a dirty site and a clean site on the same patient — for example after perineal care and before wound care. Gloves are not washed, disinfected or re-used, and gloved hands are not used to write in case notes, answer a telephone, operate a computer, open doors or handle personal mobile phones. Sterile gloves are used for surgical and aseptic procedures; examination gloves are used for routine contact.

14. Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} displays instructions at all entrances, in outpatient waiting areas and at reception in English and the local language, asking anyone with a cough or respiratory symptoms to cover the mouth and nose with a tissue when coughing or sneezing, dispose of the tissue immediately in a covered waste bin, and perform hand hygiene afterwards. Tissues, covered waste bins and handrub are provided at these points.

Symptomatic patients and attendants are offered a surgical mask and, where seating allows, are asked to sit at least one metre away from others, or are placed in a separate waiting area. Staff who develop respiratory symptoms report to their supervisor and to occupational health rather than continuing direct patient care unassessed.

15. Transmission-based precautions — activation and general rules

Where a patient is known or suspected to be infected or colonised with an agent that standard precautions alone will not contain, {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} applies transmission-based precautions in addition to standard precautions — never instead of them.

Precautions are started on clinical suspicion and are not delayed until a laboratory result confirms the organism. Any doctor or nurse may initiate them; the treating doctor and the ICN are informed within [Hospital to define] and the ICN confirms or modifies the category.

The precaution category is recorded in the patient's case record and in the nursing handover, and an instruction card showing the required PPE is displayed at the entrance to the bed space or room. The card states what staff and visitors must do; it does not name the patient's diagnosis, so that confidentiality is preserved.

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} maintains a precaution assignment register recording the patient identifier, the precaution category, the date and time of starting, the person who authorised it, and the date of discontinuation. Where more than one route of transmission applies, all relevant categories are applied together.

The personal protective equipment required by each category is consolidated here, so that the entrance card, the induction training and the audit tool all draw on one list rather than on three separate passages:

- Contact precautions — gown and gloves, put on before entering the patient's environment and removed before leaving it.
- Droplet precautions — a surgical mask, put on before entering and removed after leaving, with eye protection added where splashing or spraying towards the face is anticipated.
- Airborne precautions — a fit-tested particulate respirator (N95 or equivalent) with a user seal check on every occasion, put on before entering and removed only after leaving the room and closing the door.
- Where more than one route of transmission applies, the requirements are cumulative and the most protective respiratory item governs.

Standard precautions continue to apply underneath every category. PPE is therefore still selected on the anticipated exposure under step 10 even where the category above does not call for it — a category tells staff the minimum, never the maximum.

The assigned category is reviewed by the ICN at an interval of [Hospital to define], and additionally whenever the patient's clinical condition changes or a new microbiology result is available. Each review is recorded in the precaution assignment register with the date, the reviewer and the decision to continue, change or discontinue. A category that is never reviewed tends to outlive its indication: it holds isolation capacity that another patient needs, and it exposes the patient to the recognised harms of unnecessary isolation — reduced clinical contact, delayed investigations and lower reported wellbeing.

16. Contact precautions

Used for agents transmitted by direct contact with the patient or indirect contact with contaminated surfaces and equipment — for example multidrug-resistant organisms, Clostridioides difficile, scabies and infectious diarrhoea.

- Place the patient in a single room where available. Where a single room is not available, cohort patients infected with the same organism, or maintain spatial separation of at least one metre with a privacy curtain drawn between beds.
- Staff put on a gown and gloves before entering the patient's environment and remove them before leaving it.
- Dedicate patient-care equipment — stethoscope, thermometer, sphygmomanometer cuff — to the single patient. Where equipment must be shared, clean and disinfect it between patients with a disinfectant approved by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, following the contact time stated by the manufacturer.
- Increase the frequency of cleaning and disinfection of frequently touched surfaces in the patient zone.
- For Clostridioides difficile, staff wash hands with soap and water rather than using handrub, and a sporicidal agent is used for environmental cleaning.

17. Droplet precautions

Used for agents carried in respiratory droplets generated by coughing, sneezing, talking or certain procedures — for example influenza, pertussis, meningococcal disease, mumps and rubella.

- Place the patient in a single room where available; otherwise cohort with patients having the same infection, or maintain spatial separation of at least one metre with a curtain drawn between beds. A special air-handling system is not required and the door may remain open.
- Staff put on a surgical mask before entering the room and remove it after leaving. Eye protection is added where splashing or spraying towards the face is anticipated.
- The patient wears a surgical mask when staff are within close range and whenever moved outside the room.

18. Airborne precautions

Used for agents that stay suspended in air over distance and time — for example pulmonary and laryngeal tuberculosis, measles and chickenpox.

- Place the patient in an airborne infection isolation room (AIIR): a single room held at negative pressure relative to the adjacent corridor, with the pressure differential monitored, and with air exhausted directly outdoors or recirculated only through HEPA filtration. The ventilation rate is at least 12 air changes per hour in new construction or renovated rooms and at least 6 air changes per hour in existing facilities.
- Keep the door closed at all times except during entry and exit.
- Staff put on a fit-tested particulate respirator (N95 or equivalent) before entering and perform a user seal check on each occasion. The respirator is removed only after leaving the room and closing the door.
- Staff without immunity do not enter the room of a patient with measles or chickenpox where an immune member of staff is available.
- The patient wears a surgical mask — not a respirator — when leaving the room, and journeys outside the room are limited to those that are medically necessary.
- {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} operates a respiratory protection programme covering respirator training, fit-testing and periodic re-fit-testing. The number and location of AIIRs at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, and the arrangement to be used when no AIIR is available, are [Hospital to define].

19. Patient transport, and discontinuation of precautions

Before a patient under transmission-based precautions is moved, the receiving department is informed of the precaution category so that it is ready. The infectious site is contained — a wound is covered with a dressing, a patient on droplet or airborne precautions wears a surgical mask. Staff who transport the patient wear the PPE needed for their own contact with the patient, but change contaminated PPE and perform hand hygiene before arriving at the receiving area, so that PPE worn in the patient room is not worn through public corridors.

Precautions are discontinued only on the ICN's or treating doctor's documented decision, based on clinical resolution, the required number of negative results, or the completion of a defined treatment period. The criteria and durations applied by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} for each organism are [Hospital to define]. On discontinuation or discharge, terminal cleaning and disinfection of the room is carried out and recorded before the next patient is admitted to it.

Reference criteria for discontinuation. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} adopts the following as its standing criteria, taken from the CDC Guideline for Isolation Precautions, Appendix A. Where the treating doctor departs from a criterion for an individual patient, the departure and its reason are recorded in the case record and notified to the ICN.

- Measles — airborne precautions until 4 days after the onset of rash, and for the whole duration of the illness in an immunocompromised patient.
- Chickenpox, and disseminated herpes zoster — airborne and contact precautions until all lesions are dry and crusted.
- Pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis, confirmed — airborne precautions discontinued only when the patient is on effective therapy, is improving clinically, and has three consecutive sputum smears negative for acid-fast bacilli collected on separate days.
- Pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis, suspected — airborne precautions discontinued only when the likelihood of infectious tuberculosis is judged negligible and either another diagnosis explains the clinical syndrome or three sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli are negative, each specimen collected 8 to 24 hours apart with at least one taken in the early morning.
- Pertussis — droplet precautions until 5 days after effective antibiotic therapy has started.
- Meningococcal disease or meningitis, known or suspected — droplet precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy has started.
- Mumps — droplet precautions until 5 days after the onset of parotid swelling.
- Group A streptococcal pneumonia — droplet precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy has started, with contact precautions added where skin lesions are present.
- Clostridioides difficile — contact precautions for the duration of the illness, with hands washed using soap and running water rather than handrub because alcohol is not sporicidal, and a hypochlorite agent used for environmental cleaning where transmission continues.
- Norovirus gastroenteritis — contact precautions, with affected patients cohorted to separate air spaces and toilet facilities where an outbreak is in progress.
- Multidrug-resistant organisms — contact precautions, with the duration determined by the infection control programme of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} rather than by any fixed period, recorded as a standing decision of the ICC and reviewed when local resistance patterns shift.

Seasonal influenza is deliberately absent from the list above. The CDC appendix carries no duration entry for it and refers instead to separate seasonal influenza guidance, so {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} sets its own criterion at [Hospital to define] and reconsiders it each season rather than inheriting a figure that the source does not give.

For any organism not named above, the criterion applied is [Hospital to define], set by the ICN in consultation with the treating doctor and recorded in the precaution assignment register against that patient.

20. Safe injection practice — the core rules

Every injection given at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} follows the principle of one needle, one syringe, one patient, one time.

- Prepare and give every injection using aseptic technique, after hand hygiene.
- Use a new sterile needle and a new sterile syringe for each patient and for each entry into any medication container. Once used, both the needle and the syringe are contaminated and are discarded, even if the needle is changed.
- Never reuse a syringe to draw up a further dose for the same or another patient, and never re-enter a vial, bag or bottle with a needle or syringe that has already been used on a patient.
- Do not administer medication from a single syringe to more than one patient.
- Prepare injections in a clean, designated medication preparation area, physically separated from any area where contaminated items are placed.
- Prepare each dose as close as practicable to the time of administration; do not carry pre-drawn, unlabelled syringes on a trolley for later use.
- Label every prepared syringe with the drug name, strength, and the date and time of preparation.

Patients and attendants at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} are entitled to see the needle and syringe being opened from an intact sterile pack.

21. Vials, ampoules and medication preparation

- Single-dose and single-use vials, ampoules, and bags or bottles of intravenous solution are used for one dose for one patient and are then discarded, even if unused product remains. Leftover contents are never pooled or saved for a later dose or another patient.
- Multi-dose vials are avoided where a single-dose presentation exists. Where a multi-dose vial must be used, it is dedicated to a single patient wherever possible, and is kept out of the immediate patient treatment area so it cannot be contaminated by spray or splash.
- Before each entry into a multi-dose vial, disinfect the rubber septum with 70% alcohol and allow it to dry. Enter only with a sterile needle and a sterile syringe.
- Write the date of first entry on every multi-dose vial and discard it by the manufacturer's stated beyond-use date, or immediately if sterility is compromised or is in question.
- Bags and bottles of intravenous solution are not used as a common source of supply for more than one patient.

22. Infusion and intravascular device practice

- Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic technique for insertion of, and every access to, any intravascular device.
- Disinfect the skin at the insertion site with the antiseptic specified by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} and allow it to dry fully before puncture.
- Disinfect the hub, port or connector before every access, and allow it to dry.
- Cover the insertion site with a sterile dressing, and record on it the date of insertion and the date the dressing was applied.
- Inspect the site at least once every shift for redness, swelling, tenderness, discharge or dressing failure, and record the finding in the nursing notes.
- Remove any device as soon as it is no longer clinically needed. Review the continued need for every intravascular device at each daily round and record the decision.
- Replace administration sets at the frequency defined by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} for each fluid type — [Hospital to define].
- Insertion and maintenance bundle compliance is audited using a structured checklist, at a frequency of [Hospital to define], with results and corrective actions tabled at the ICC.

23. Staff health and immunisation — protection before exposure

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} protects its staff before an exposure occurs, not only after one. Occupational health, or the designated officer where no separate function exists, maintains an immunisation record for every member of staff and for every contracted or outsourced worker who may come into contact with blood, body fluids, biomedical waste or food.

Hepatitis B vaccination is offered to all staff with any potential exposure to blood or body fluids, at no cost to the individual, and is arranged at induction rather than deferred. The vaccine is given intramuscularly in the deltoid as a three-dose series at 0, 1 and 6 months.

Serological confirmation of protection follows the series: anti-HBs is tested one to two months after the final dose, and a level of 10 mIU/mL or above is taken as protective. Staff whose level is below this threshold are offered a repeat course and retested. A member of staff who does not respond to a second complete series is regarded as susceptible, is counselled accordingly, and is managed on the assumption that hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis will be required after any significant exposure. Results are recorded against the individual and are used at the time of an exposure so that a decision is not delayed while immunity is established.

Other vaccinations offered by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} are:
- typhoid vaccination for food handlers and dietary staff;
- tetanus-containing vaccine (Td or tetanus toxoid) for staff who handle biomedical waste and for others at risk of contaminated injury; and
- any further vaccine indicated by national policy, by the individual's role, or by an outbreak situation — [Hospital to define].

Vaccination is offered and encouraged, and reasons for declining are recorded on a signed declination form so that {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} can demonstrate the offer was made. Staff with an illness transmissible to patients report to occupational health and are assigned to duties away from direct patient contact until fit, and are not permitted to work through an infectious illness on the basis of staffing pressure.

24. Sharps safety and management of exposure to blood and body fluids

Preventing the injury:
- Needles are never recapped. Where recapping is genuinely unavoidable, the single-handed scoop technique is used and never a two-handed technique.
- Used needles are not bent, broken, sheared or removed from the syringe by hand.
- The person who uses a sharp disposes of it, personally and immediately, into a puncture-proof, leak-proof, tamper-proof container placed within arm's reach at the point of use. Sharps are never passed hand to hand, left on a trolley or bed, or carried to a distant container.
- Sharps containers are closed and replaced when filled to the marked line — approximately three quarters full — and are never overfilled or reopened.
- Safety-engineered devices with needle-retraction or shielding are used where {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} has adopted them; a hands-free neutral zone is used for passing sharps during procedures.

Immediately after a needlestick injury, a cut from a contaminated sharp, or a splash of blood or body fluid on to broken skin or a mucous membrane:
1. Wash the site with soap and running water. The wound is not squeezed to express fluid, is not scrubbed and is not sucked, and no caustic agent such as bleach is applied to it. An antiseptic or disinfectant is never injected into the wound. Applying an antiseptic to the site after washing is not prohibited, and remains common practice in India, but there is no evidence that it reduces transmission and it is never a substitute for washing. Irrigate eyes or other mucous membranes with clean water or normal saline.
2. Report at once to the supervisor and the ICN or occupational health. The exposure is not deferred to the end of a shift, because prophylaxis is time-critical.
3. Record the exposure in the sharps injury register with the date, time, place, device, procedure, circumstances and depth or type of exposure.
4. Assess the source. With appropriate consent and counselling, test the source patient for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and check the exposed worker's baseline status and hepatitis B immunity from the immunisation record held under step 23.

Prophylaxis and follow-up:
- HIV: where prophylaxis is indicated, the first dose is given as soon as possible, ideally within hours of the exposure and preferably within two, and is not started beyond 72 hours after the exposure, after which it is not considered effective. This is the same rule, in the same words, as the occupational health and post-exposure policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, which owns the detail; if either document changes it, the other is changed in the same pass. The course runs for 28 days, with adherence support and follow-up testing.
- Hepatitis B: prophylaxis is started immediately and ideally within 24 hours. Hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine are given according to the exposed worker's immunity status and, when given together, are injected at separate sites. The interval within which prophylaxis remains useful after a percutaneous exposure is unlikely to extend beyond 7 days, so delay is not acceptable.
- Hepatitis C: no vaccine and no post-exposure prophylaxis exist. Management is baseline and follow-up testing, with prompt referral for treatment if infection is detected.
- The specific regimens, the responsible officer, the out-of-hours pathway and the follow-up testing schedule used by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} are set out in its Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Protocol — [Hospital to define].

Every exposure is reviewed at the ICC to identify the device, procedure, area and time of shift involved, so that the cause is corrected. Reporting is not penalised; under-reporting is treated as the more serious failure.

25. Management of blood and body fluid spills

Every clinical area of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} keeps a spill kit that is accessible without leaving the area, and staff on duty are able to locate and use it. The kit contains gloves, a plastic apron, a mask and eye protection, absorbent material, a scoop or forceps and a small dustpan for any broken glass, the hospital's chlorine-releasing disinfectant with a measuring aid, yellow biomedical waste bags, and a laminated instruction card.

A spill is dealt with by the staff of the area where it happened, immediately, and is not left for the next housekeeping round. The procedure is:

1. Restrict access to the area and prevent anyone from walking through the spill.
2. Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves, apron, mask and eye protection.
3. Pick up any broken glass or sharp fragment first, using a scoop, forceps or dustpan — never with the hands, even when gloved — and place it directly into the sharps container.
4. Cover the spill with absorbent material and remove the bulk of the visible organic matter. This step comes before disinfection and is not optional: chlorine-releasing disinfectants are substantially inactivated by blood and protein, so applying disinfectant on to an uncleaned spill does not reliably work.
5. Apply the chlorine-releasing disinfectant at the concentration specified in the disinfection policy of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} and leave it for the full contact time stated by the manufacturer. As a guide to the order of magnitude involved, published guidance uses a 1:10 dilution of 5.25–6.15% household bleach — roughly 5,000–6,150 ppm available chlorine — for a large spill, and a 1:100 dilution — roughly 500–615 ppm — for small drops on a non-critical surface. Indian practice commonly specifies a 1% sodium hypochlorite solution for blood spills. The exact product, working concentration and contact time used at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} are [Hospital to define] and are stated on the spill kit instruction card so that no one has to estimate at the time.
6. Wipe up the disinfectant with fresh absorbent material and clean the surface with detergent and water.
7. Place all contaminated absorbent material, disposable cleaning items and used PPE into the yellow biomedical waste stream. Remove PPE in the sequence given in step 12 and perform hand hygiene.
8. Record the spill and, where any person was exposed, manage that exposure under step 24 and report it as an incident.

Hypochlorite is not applied directly to a urine spill. Urine contains ammonia, and bleach reacting with ammonia releases chloramine gas, which is toxic on inhalation and dangerous in an enclosed space such as a bathroom or sluice room. Urine spills are absorbed and cleaned with detergent and water first, and disinfected afterwards only once the urine has been removed. Hypochlorite is corrosive to metal, so metal surfaces and equipment are decontaminated with an alternative agent named in the disinfection policy — [Hospital to define].

All clinical, housekeeping and support staff of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} are trained in spill management and are able to demonstrate the procedure on request, including to an assessor.

26. Segregation of biomedical waste at the point of generation

Segregation happens at the bedside or procedure trolley at the moment the waste is produced — never later by a second person. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} follows the four-colour system of the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (India):

- YELLOW — non-chlorinated plastic bag or container. Human and animal anatomical waste; soiled waste such as dressings, cotton, bandages and other items contaminated with blood or body fluids; expired and discarded medicines; chemical waste; discarded linen contaminated with blood or body fluids; and microbiology, biotechnology and clinical laboratory waste. Disposal: incineration, plasma pyrolysis, or deep burial where permitted.
- RED — non-chlorinated plastic bag or container. Contaminated recyclable waste: disposable items such as tubing, bottles, intravenous tubes and sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes without needles, and gloves. Disposal: autoclaving, microwaving or hydroclaving, followed by mutilation or shredding, then recycling through a registered recycler.
- WHITE (translucent) — puncture-proof, leak-proof, tamper-proof container. Waste sharps including metals: needles, fixed-needle syringes, scalpels, blades, and any contaminated sharp object capable of causing a puncture or cut. Disposal: autoclaving or dry-heat sterilisation followed by shredding, mutilation, or encapsulation.
- BLUE — cardboard box with blue marking, or puncture-proof container. Glassware, including broken, discarded and contaminated glass, medicine vials and ampoules; and metallic body implants. Disposal: disinfection or autoclaving, then recycling.

Untreated biomedical waste is not stored at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} beyond 48 hours. Colour-coded bins with the correct liners, foot-operated lids and category charts are placed in every clinical area. All staff who generate waste — including doctors, nurses, technicians and housekeeping — are trained in segregation, and segregation errors are audited by the ICN at a frequency of [Hospital to define]. The name of the common biomedical waste treatment facility used by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, the collection schedule and the authorisation details are [Hospital to define].

28. Implementing the antimicrobial usage policy and monitoring rational use

The policy is enforced at the point of dispensing and reviewed after the fact.

- Every antimicrobial order records the indication, the dose, the route and either a stop date or a review date. Orders without these are queried by the ward pharmacist before dispensing.
- Restricted agents are dispensed only against a recorded authorisation. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} maintains a restricted antimicrobial approval register capturing the prescriber, the patient identifier, the agent, the indication, the authorising person and the date.
- The pharmacy produces a consumption report by ward and by drug class at a frequency of [Hospital to define], expressed in defined daily doses (DDD) per 100 bed-days using the WHO ATC/DDD methodology so that figures are comparable between wards and over time.
- Prescription audits are conducted on a random sample of inpatient case records per clinical area, at a sample size and frequency of [Hospital to define], assessing whether the choice of agent, the dose, the route and the duration matched the policy and whether cultures were sent before therapy started. Findings are recorded in an audit register and given to the individual prescriber as feedback within [Hospital to define].
- The microbiology laboratory of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} produces a cumulative antibiogram at least annually. The ICC reviews it and revises the empirical regimens in the policy where local resistance patterns have shifted; the revision is recorded with a new version number and effective date.
- Consumption trends, audit findings, resistance patterns and the outcome of corrective actions are tabled at every ICC meeting and minuted.

29. Antibiotic stewardship programme

Note on status: the requirement for a stewardship programme sits at Excellence level within this standard and is above the baseline expected of every organisation. It calls for a functioning programme; it does not by itself require a standing committee. {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} nevertheless constitutes an Antimicrobial Stewardship Team (AST) as the practical means of running and evidencing the programme.

The programme at {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} is built on the recognised core elements of hospital antibiotic stewardship — leadership commitment, accountability, pharmacy expertise, action, tracking, reporting and education:

- Leadership commitment — senior management of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} formally commits the necessary staff time, information technology and budget, in writing.
- Accountability — a single named leader is accountable for the programme's outcomes. The AST membership, its lead, its meeting frequency and its quorum are [Hospital to define]; the team is typically led by a physician with infectious disease or microbiology expertise and includes a clinical pharmacist and the ICN.
- Pharmacy expertise — a named pharmacist co-leads improvement in antimicrobial use.
- Action — the programme runs at least one intervention with a documented method. Prospective audit and feedback is the recommended approach: the AST reviews every patient still receiving antimicrobial therapy beyond 72 hours, and issues written recommendations to the prescriber that are filed in the record. A formal antibiotic time-out at 48 to 72 hours, at which therapy is reassessed against culture results, is documented for every patient on antimicrobials.
- Tracking — the AST tracks process measures (adherence to the policy, documentation of indication and duration, time-out completion) and outcome measures (DDD per 100 bed-days, restricted agent use, rates of Clostridioides difficile infection and of resistant organisms, and culture positivity).
- Reporting — trend data is reported to prescribers and to hospital leadership at a frequency of [Hospital to define], at least quarterly.
- Education — prescribers, nurses and pharmacists receive education on resistance and on optimal prescribing, with attendance recorded.

The AST has a written charter stating its purpose, membership, authority and measurable goals — for example a reduction in days of therapy or in the use of a named restricted agent. Baseline values and targets are [Hospital to define].

30. Surveillance of healthcare-associated infections — interface with this policy

{{HOSPITAL_NAME}} conducts surveillance for healthcare-associated infection, because the practices set out in this policy can only be shown to work by measuring their result. Surveillance covers, as a minimum, ventilator-associated pneumonia or ventilator-associated events, central line-associated bloodstream infection, catheter-associated urinary tract infection, and surgical site infection.

Surveillance uses standard, published case definitions applied consistently, rather than definitions devised locally, so that rates mean the same thing from month to month and can be compared externally. The definitions and methods published in the Patient Safety Component Manual of the CDC's National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) are a recognised source for this purpose. Rates are expressed against the appropriate denominator — device-days for device-associated infection, and procedures for surgical site infection — and not against admissions or bed-days.

Surveillance findings are reported to the ICC and to the clinical areas concerned, and are used to direct the corrective actions required elsewhere in this policy: a rise in device-associated infection triggers re-audit of the relevant bundle under step 22, and a rise in resistant organisms is taken to the AST under step 29.

The full surveillance methodology of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} — case definitions in use, data collection responsibility, denominators, rate calculation, reporting frequency, benchmarks and validation — is set out in the organisation's infection prevention and control programme document and its quality indicator framework, not in this policy. Those details are [Hospital to define].

31. Training, orientation and competency

Every new employee of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} — clinical, support, housekeeping, dietary, security, and contracted or outsourced personnel — receives infection control training during induction, before independent patient contact. Content covers standard precautions, hand hygiene moments and technique, PPE selection and the donning and doffing sequences, transmission-based precautions, safe injection practice, sharps handling, exposure reporting and post-exposure prophylaxis, blood and body fluid spill management, staff immunisation entitlements, and biomedical waste segregation.

Refresher training is repeated at a frequency of [Hospital to define], and after any change to this policy. Training is assessed by return demonstration, not attendance alone: staff physically demonstrate hand hygiene technique, the doffing sequence and the spill management procedure to an assessor, and the result is recorded against the individual's name with the date and the assessor's signature. Staff who do not pass are retrained and reassessed before resuming independent practice.

Attendance registers, assessment records and competency scores are retained by {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} and are available for review.

33. Review of this policy

This policy is reviewed at least once every year by the ICC of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}}, and earlier if there is a change in national regulation or in recognised international guidance, a significant infection control incident or outbreak, a material shift in the hospital's antibiogram, or the introduction of a new clinical service. Each review is minuted with the names of those present, and any revision is issued with an incremented version number, a new effective date, and withdrawal of superseded copies from clinical areas. The document owner, approving authority and controlled-copy distribution list are [Hospital to define].
responsibility:
Hospital leadership of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} — provides the budget, staffing, facilities and infrastructure the programme requires, including hand hygiene consumables and hands-free taps, PPE, safety-engineered sharps devices, spill kits, staff vaccination, isolation capability and waste handling arrangements; formally commits support for antimicrobial stewardship in writing; and reviews programme performance data.

Infection Control Committee (ICC) — approves this policy and the antimicrobial usage policy; reviews compliance audits, healthcare-associated infection surveillance data, sharps injuries and spill incidents, waste segregation findings, antimicrobial consumption and resistance trends; records named corrective actions with owners and due dates; and verifies closure of those actions at the following meeting.

Infection Control Nurse / designated infection control officer — runs the programme day to day; conducts and documents hand hygiene, standard precautions, PPE, bundle and waste segregation audits; confirms or modifies transmission-based precaution categories and maintains the precaution register; investigates sharps injuries, exposures, spills and breaches; compiles surveillance data; delivers training; and reports to the ICC.

Occupational health / designated staff health officer — maintains the immunisation record for every member of staff and contracted worker; arranges hepatitis B vaccination and post-vaccination anti-HBs testing and records the results; holds signed declination forms; manages occupational exposures including source assessment, prophylaxis within the required time window and follow-up testing; and assesses fitness for duty of staff with transmissible illness or hand dermatitis.

Head of each clinical department / nursing in-charge — is accountable for compliance within their own area; ensures staff are trained and competent before independent practice; ensures a stocked spill kit is available and accessible; addresses audit findings for their area; and keeps infection control as a standing item in departmental meetings.

Treating doctors and prescribers — apply standard and transmission-based precautions personally; prescribe within the antimicrobial usage policy; record indication, dose, route and stop or review date with every antimicrobial order; send cultures before starting therapy where clinically feasible; de-escalate on receipt of results; and participate in the antibiotic time-out.

Nursing staff — perform hand hygiene at the five moments; select, don and doff PPE correctly; maintain aseptic technique for all injections, infusions and device care; segregate waste and dispose of sharps at the point of use; contain and decontaminate spills occurring in their area; maintain the precaution register and precaution signage; and inspect and document intravascular device sites each shift.

Pharmacy / ward pharmacist — maintains the antimicrobial formulary and the restricted agent list; queries antimicrobial orders lacking an indication or stop date before dispensing; maintains the restricted antimicrobial approval register; produces consumption reports in DDD per 100 bed-days; and provides pharmacy expertise to the stewardship team.

Microbiology laboratory — processes cultures, reports sensitivities promptly, produces and circulates the cumulative antibiogram at least annually, supports surveillance case-finding, and alerts the ICN to organisms of infection control significance.

Antimicrobial Stewardship Team (AST), where constituted — runs prospective audit and feedback, issues and files written recommendations to prescribers, tracks process and outcome metrics, and reports trends to prescribers and leadership. Membership, lead, meeting frequency and quorum are [Hospital to define].

Housekeeping and sanitation staff — carry out routine, enhanced and terminal cleaning and disinfection to the specified method and contact time; assist with spill decontamination under the direction of the area in-charge; check and refill hand hygiene dispensers each shift and log the check; and collect, transport and hand over segregated biomedical waste without re-sorting it.

Maintenance and engineering — installs and maintains hands-free taps, handwash basins, AIIR ventilation and pressure monitoring, and rectifies dispenser and plumbing faults reported through the dispenser check log.

Central sterile supply / equipment care — reprocesses reusable instruments and equipment to validated parameters and maintains the associated records.

Human resources and training — ensures every new joiner, including contracted and outsourced personnel, receives infection control induction and is offered the applicable vaccinations before independent patient contact, and maintains attendance and competency records.

Every individual working in or entering a clinical area — complies with this policy, reports breaches, sharps injuries, exposures, spills and near misses, and is empowered to stop an unsafe practice regardless of the seniority of the person involved.

2. World Health Organization — "Your 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" poster and the WHO hand hygiene observation method / observation form.
3. World Health Organization — "How to Handrub? With alcohol-based formulation" technique poster (20-30 seconds).

5. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Standard Precautions for All Patient Care, and STRIVE module "The Basics of Standard Precautions".
6. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Guideline for Isolation Precautions: Precautions to Prevent Transmission of Infectious Agents in Healthcare Settings (contact, droplet and airborne precautions; airborne infection isolation room requirements).

10. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Hepatitis B Vaccine Administration, and recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination and post-vaccination serologic testing of healthcare personnel.
11. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / National Clinician Consultation Center — PEP Quick Guide for Bloodborne Pathogen Exposures, and guidance on occupational hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis.
12. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities: Chemical Disinfectants, and Environmental Services guidance (management of blood spills; inactivation of germicides by organic matter; bleach dilutions).
13. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Patient Safety Component Manual (standard surveillance definitions for CLABSI, CAUTI, VAE/VAP and SSI).
14. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Core Elements of Hospital Antibiotic Stewardship Programs (2019 update) and Priorities for Hospital Core Element Implementation (2022).
15. World Health Organization — ATC/DDD Toolkit: Defined Daily Dose (DDD) methodology, WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics Methodology, Oslo.
16. World Health Organization — AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) classification of antibiotics.
17. Government of India, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change — Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended, Schedule I (colour-coded segregation categories, treatment and disposal options, and the 48-hour storage limit for untreated waste).
18. Central Pollution Control Board — Guidelines for Handling, Treatment and Disposal of Waste Generated during Healthcare Activities.

Internal documents of {{HOSPITAL_NAME}} referenced by this policy: Infection Control Committee terms of reference; Infection Prevention and Control Programme document and quality indicator framework; Antimicrobial Usage Policy; Hospital Disinfection Policy; Biomedical Waste Management Plan; Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Protocol; Employee Health and Immunisation Policy; Housekeeping and Environmental Cleaning SOP; Central Sterile Supply Department SOP; and the Records Retention Policy. universal_facts_checklist:
UNIVERSAL FACTS INCLUDED — FOR REVIEWER VERIFICATION

HAND HYGIENE
1. WHO "My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" — all five moments with WHEN and WHY, and the rule that Moments 1-2 precede the action and 3-5 follow it. Verified via WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care, "The WHO Multimodal Hand Hygiene Improvement Strategy" (NCBI Bookshelf NBK144032) and the WHO "Your 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" poster (who.int).
2. Alcohol-based handrub technique — apply a palmful into a cupped hand, then the six rubbing movements: palm to palm; right palm over left dorsum with interlaced fingers and vice versa; palm to palm with fingers interlaced; backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked; rotational rubbing of the thumb clasped in the opposite palm; rotational backwards-and-forwards rubbing of clasped fingertips in the opposite palm. Ends with "once dry, hands are safe". Verified via WHO "How to Handrub" poster (who.int) and an independent transcription of the same WHO steps (ubentingoedehanden.be).
3. Handrub duration 20-30 seconds. Verified via WHO "How to Handrub" poster.
4. Handwash technique — wet hands, apply soap to cover all surfaces, same six rubbing movements, rinse, dry with a single-use towel, use the towel to turn off the tap. Verified via WHO "How to Handwash" poster (who.int).
5. Handwash duration 40-60 seconds. Verified via WHO "How to Handwash" poster and WHO public guidance.
6. Soap and water required in place of handrub when hands are visibly soiled, and for spore-forming organisms (C. difficile) where alcohol is not reliably effective. Verified via WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care (NCBI NBK144035) and CDC infection control guidance.
7. Hand hygiene compliance formula = (actions / opportunities) x 100, by direct observation from a trained and validated observer, session length approximately 20 minutes +/- 10. Verified via WHO hand hygiene observation method / WHO Guidelines "Hand hygiene as a performance indicator" (NCBI NBK144028).

STANDARD PRECAUTIONS AND PPE
8. Components of standard precautions — hand hygiene, PPE, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, safe injection practice, sharps safety, equipment decontamination, environmental cleaning, safe linen handling, waste disposal; applied to all patients regardless of diagnosis. Verified via CDC Standard Precautions guidance (cdc.gov) and CDC STRIVE "The Basics of Standard Precautions".
9. PPE DONNING sequence — hand hygiene, gown, mask/respirator, goggles or face shield, gloves over the gown cuff. Verified via CDC "Sequence for Donning and Doffing Personal Protective Equipment" poster.
10. PPE DOFFING sequence — gloves, goggles/face shield, gown, then leave the room, then mask/respirator, then hand hygiene; mask removed outside the room; front of mask never touched. Verified via the same CDC poster and CDC PPE guidance.
11. Gloves supplement and never replace hand hygiene; hand hygiene before donning and after removal; change between patients and between dirty and clean sites on the same patient. Verified via WHO hand hygiene guidelines and CDC standard precautions guidance.

TRANSMISSION-BASED PRECAUTIONS
12. Three categories — contact, droplet, airborne; applied IN ADDITION to standard precautions. Verified via CDC "Precautions to Prevent Transmission of Infectious Agents" (cdc.gov).
13. Droplet precautions — surgical mask on entry, single room or cohorting, spatial separation of at least one metre, no special air handling, door may stay open. Verified via CDC transmission-based precautions guidance and StatPearls (NCBI NBK551555).
14. Airborne precautions — AIIR with monitored negative pressure; at least 12 air changes per hour for new construction/renovation and at least 6 for existing facilities; air exhausted outdoors or HEPA-filtered before recirculation; fit-tested N95 or higher respirator with user seal check; respiratory protection programme with fit-testing required. Verified via CDC "Precautions to Prevent Transmission of Infectious Agents" and CDC environmental control "Air" guidance.
15. Non-immune staff should not enter measles/varicella rooms where an immune worker is available; patient wears a surgical mask (not a respirator) during transport. Verified via CDC transmission-based precautions guidance.

INJECTION AND INFUSION SAFETY
16. "One needle, one syringe, only one time" — CDC / Safe Injection Practices Coalition One & Only Campaign. Verified via CDC Injection Safety, "Safe Injection Practices to Prevent Transmission of Infections to Patients".
17. Single-dose vials/ampoules/IV bags used for one dose for one patient then discarded; contents never pooled. Verified via the same CDC guidance.
18. Multi-dose vials — sterile needle and syringe for every entry, disinfect the rubber septum with 70% alcohol and let it dry, dedicate to a single patient where possible, keep out of the immediate patient treatment area, date on first entry, discard by the manufacturer's beyond-use date. Verified via CDC injection safety guidance ("Preventing Unsafe Injection Practices").
19. Never re-enter a vial/bag/bottle with a needle or syringe already used on a patient; a used syringe is contaminated even if the needle is changed. Verified via CDC injection safety guidance.
20. No recapping of needles; single-handed scoop technique only if recapping is unavoidable; no bending, breaking or hand removal of needles; user disposes of the sharp immediately into a puncture-proof container at the point of use; replace containers at approximately three-quarters full. Verified via CDC sharps safety / standard precautions guidance.

STAFF IMMUNISATION AND POST-EXPOSURE MANAGEMENT (ADDED REV 2)
21. Hepatitis B vaccination for healthcare personnel — three-dose series given intramuscularly in the deltoid at 0, 1 and 6 months. Verified via CDC "Hepatitis B Vaccine Administration" (cdc.gov) and WHO/CDC healthcare worker guidance.
22. Post-vaccination serologic testing — anti-HBs measured 1 to 2 months after the final dose; a level of 10 mIU/mL or above is protective. Verified via CDC Hepatitis B vaccine administration guidance.
23. Non-responders — repeat series and retest; a person who does not respond after a second complete series is managed as susceptible and will require post-exposure prophylaxis. CONSISTENT with CDC guidance on non-responders but NOT separately verified in a dedicated search; reviewer to confirm this sub-point against the current CDC healthcare personnel recommendations.
24. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis — first dose as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, and no later than 72 hours after exposure; 28-day course. Verified via CDC/National Clinician Consultation Center "PEP Quick Guide for Bloodborne Pathogen Exposures".
25. Hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis — start immediately, ideally within 24 hours; the interval within which it remains effective after a percutaneous exposure is unlikely to exceed 7 days; when HBIG and vaccine are given together they must go at separate body sites. Verified via CDC/University of Washington "Occupational HBV Postexposure Prophylaxis" core concepts and the NCCC PEP Quick Guide.
26. Hepatitis C — no vaccine and no post-exposure prophylaxis; management is baseline and follow-up testing with referral for treatment. Well-established CDC position; NOT separately verified in a dedicated search. Reviewer to confirm.
27. Do not squeeze, scrub or apply caustic agents (bleach, antiseptic) to a sharps wound; irrigate mucous membranes with water or saline. Standard occupational-exposure first aid, consistent with WHO/CDC exposure management guidance. Reviewer to confirm phrasing is acceptable.
>> NOTE: typhoid vaccination for food handlers and tetanus-containing vaccine for biomedical waste handlers are NABH-DERIVED, not universal WHO/CDC recommendations for healthcare workers. Source: NABH Hospital Infection Control Checklist (E.-HIB_CHECK-04.12), row 6. They are included because NABH's own checklist asks for them, and are written as an offer rather than as a universal clinical standard. All other vaccines are left as [Hospital to define] against national policy.

BLOOD AND BODY FLUID SPILL MANAGEMENT (ADDED REV 2)
28. Remove visible organic matter with absorbent material BEFORE applying disinfectant, because hypochlorites and other germicides are substantially inactivated by blood and protein. Verified via CDC "Chemical Disinfectants" (Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization) and CDC "Environmental Services" infection control guidance.
29. Concentration guidance — a 1:10 dilution of 5.25-6.15% household bleach (approximately 5,000-6,150 ppm available chlorine) for large blood spills, and a 1:100 dilution (approximately 500-615 ppm) for small drops on non-critical surfaces. Verified via CDC Chemical Disinfectants guidance.
>> REVIEWER FLAG: the draft ALSO notes that Indian practice commonly specifies 1% sodium hypochlorite (10,000 ppm) for blood spills. That 1% figure is presented in the draft as common Indian practice, NOT as a CDC number, and the actual working concentration and contact time are left as [Hospital to define] deliberately, so the hospital's own disinfection policy governs. Please confirm you are comfortable with both figures appearing side by side — the alternative is to drop the CDC dilutions and carry only "[Hospital to define]".
30. Hypochlorite is corrosive to metals. Verified via CDC Chemical Disinfectants guidance.
31. Hypochlorite is not applied directly to urine spills. Urine contains ammonia; bleach reacting with ammonia releases CHLORAMINE gas (not chlorine gas), which causes eye, nose, throat and chest irritation and, at higher exposure, chemical pneumonitis and pulmonary oedema. Verified via Washington State Department of Health, "Dangers of Mixing Bleach with Cleaners" (doh.wa.gov), which names urine explicitly as an ammonia source, supported by Duke University sodium hypochlorite safety documentation and published chloramine inhalation case literature (PubMed 9503902). CORRECTION FROM REV 2: the rev 2 draft said "chlorine gas"; the correct product is chloramine. Draft text corrected.
32. Broken glass is picked up mechanically (scoop, forceps, dustpan) and never by hand, gloved or not. Standard sharps-safety practice consistent with CDC sharps guidance.

HEALTHCARE-ASSOCIATED INFECTION SURVEILLANCE — BRIEF POINTER ONLY (ADDED REV 2)
33. The four core HAI types under surveillance — ventilator-associated pneumonia / ventilator-associated events, central line-associated bloodstream infection, catheter-associated urinary tract infection, and surgical site infection. Verified via CDC NHSN Patient Safety Component Manual (cdc.gov/nhsn), which covers CLABSI, CAUTI, VAE/PedVAE, VAP and SSI modules.
34. Standard published case definitions must be used rather than locally devised ones, and device-associated rates use device-days as the denominator while SSI uses procedures. Verified via CDC NHSN Patient Safety Component Manual.
>> SCOPE NOTE: step 31 is deliberately a POINTER, not a methodology. Full surveillance method (case definitions in use, data collection, denominators, rate calculation, benchmarking, validation) is explicitly deferred to the IPC programme document and the quality indicator framework, and is recorded as a TODO against CQI in scripts/master-policy-todos.md.

BIOMEDICAL WASTE (INDIA)
35. Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 four-colour segregation — YELLOW (anatomical, soiled, expired medicines, chemical, contaminated linen, laboratory waste; non-chlorinated bag; incineration/plasma pyrolysis/deep burial); RED (contaminated recyclables - tubing, IV sets, catheters, urine bags, needle-free syringes, gloves; non-chlorinated bag; autoclave/microwave/hydroclave then shred and recycle); WHITE TRANSLUCENT (sharps and metals; puncture-proof, leak-proof, tamper-proof container; autoclave or dry heat then shred/mutilate/encapsulate); BLUE (glassware, vials, ampoules, metallic implants; cardboard box with blue marking; disinfect then recycle). Verified via PIB Government of India release on BMW Rules 2016 and CPCB Guidelines for Handling, Treatment and Disposal of Waste Generated during Healthcare Activities (June 2018).
36. Untreated biomedical waste not stored beyond 48 hours. Verified via BMW Rules 2016 text (state pollution control board publications of the Rules as amended).

>> REVIEWER FLAG (carried from rev 1): item 35 was confirmed from official CPCB/PIB summaries of Schedule I, because every full-text Schedule I PDF I attempted was image-only and could not be machine-read. The four colours, waste types, container types and disposal routes above are consistent across those sources, but please cross-check the exact Schedule I wording once against the current CPCB table before this draft is approved, in case of any amendment.

ANTIMICROBIAL USE AND STEWARDSHIP
37. Seven CDC Core Elements of Hospital Antibiotic Stewardship Programs — leadership commitment, accountability, pharmacy expertise, action, tracking, reporting, education (2019 update; "pharmacy expertise" replaced the earlier "drug expertise"). Verified via CDC "Core Elements of Hospital Antibiotic Stewardship Programs" (cdc.gov).
38. Prospective audit and feedback, and the 48-72 hour antibiotic time-out, as recognised stewardship interventions. Verified via CDC Core Elements guidance.
39. DDD (defined daily dose) per 100 bed-days as the standard hospital antimicrobial consumption metric, under WHO ATC/DDD methodology maintained by the WHO Collaborating Centre, Oslo. Verified via WHO ATC/DDD Toolkit, "Defined Daily Dose (DDD)" (who.int).
40. WHO AWaRe classification — Access, Watch, Reserve — as a framework for structuring the antimicrobial list and setting use targets. Verified via WHO AWaRe classification references.
41. Cumulative antibiogram updated at least annually to guide empirical therapy. Standard microbiology practice; consistent with CDC Core Elements "action" and "tracking".

TRANSMISSION-BASED PRECAUTIONS — DURATION AND DISCONTINUATION (added 2026-08-13)
Source for facts 42-52: CDC, Guideline for Isolation Precautions: Preventing Transmission of Infectious Agents in Healthcare Settings (2007), Appendix A "Type and Duration of Precautions Recommended for Selected Infections and Conditions", current version dated 2 February 2025. Read from the source table directly rather than from a search summary or from recollection. These were added to step 19, which previously carried the BASIS for discontinuation but left every actual duration as "[Hospital to define]".
42. Measles — airborne precautions until 4 days after onset of rash; duration of illness in an immunocompromised patient.
43. Chickenpox, and disseminated herpes zoster — airborne plus contact precautions until all lesions are dry and crusted.
44. Pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis, CONFIRMED — discontinue only when the patient is on effective therapy, is improving clinically, and has three consecutive sputum smears negative for acid-fast bacilli collected on separate days.
45. Pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis, SUSPECTED — discontinue only when infectious tuberculosis is judged negligible and either another diagnosis explains the clinical syndrome or three acid-fast bacilli smears are negative, each specimen collected 8 to 24 hours apart with at least one an early morning specimen. Note the two entries differ; the draft carries both because a suspected case is the commoner situation on a ward.
46. Pertussis — droplet precautions until 5 days after initiation of effective antibiotic therapy.
47. Meningococcal disease or meningitis, known or suspected — droplet precautions until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy.
48. Mumps — droplet precautions until 5 days after onset of parotid swelling. Appendix A carries an explicit October 2017 update recording HICPAC's change from 9 days to 5; the 5-day figure is the current one.
49. Group A streptococcal pneumonia — droplet precautions until 24 hours after initiation of effective therapy, with contact precautions added where skin lesions are present.
50. Clostridioides difficile — contact precautions for the duration of illness; handwashing with soap and water preferred because alcohol is not sporicidal; hypochlorite for cleaning where transmission continues. Consistent with fact 5 already in this checklist.
51. Norovirus gastroenteritis — contact plus standard precautions, with cohorting to separate air spaces and toilet facilities during an outbreak. Appendix A carries an April 2019 update changing the type of precaution from "Standard" to "Contact + Standard"; the draft states the updated position.
52. Multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, VISA/VRSA, ESBL producers, resistant S. pneumoniae) — contact precautions, with NO fixed duration given. Appendix A leaves the duration to the infection control programme on local, state, regional or national recommendations, so the draft makes it a standing ICC decision rather than inventing a period.

REVIEWER TO NOTE — A DELIBERATE OMISSION (2026-08-13)
Seasonal influenza is NOT given a duration in step 19, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. The current Appendix A carries no duration entry for seasonal influenza — the row reads "n/a" and refers the reader to separate CDC seasonal influenza guidance. The commonly quoted figure (7 days from onset, or 24 hours after fever resolves, whichever is longer) comes from that separate guidance and NOT from Appendix A. Rather than attribute a figure to a source that does not carry it, step 19 states the omission openly and leaves the criterion to the hospital at "[Hospital to define]", to be reconsidered each season. If a later revision wants a fixed figure, cite the seasonal influenza guidance specifically — do not cite Appendix A for it.

NABH-DERIVED POINTS (not universal facts — flagged for the reviewer)
- Hands-free taps (elbow, foot or sensor operated) MANDATORY in the OT scrub area, and preferred at other clinical handwash basins; basins of adequate size and depth. Source: NABH Hospital Infection Control Checklist (E.-HIB_CHECK-04.12), row 4. This is a NABH expectation, NOT a WHO/CDC universal fact — the draft states it as a hospital requirement without attributing it to WHO or CDC. Written in original wording.
- Typhoid vaccine for food handlers and tetanus-containing vaccine for biomedical waste handlers — see the note under item 27 above. Same source, row 6.
- HIC.2.g (antibiotic stewardship programme) is at EXCELLENCE level, not Core or Commitment. Step 30 states this explicitly and notes that the OE requires a programme, not necessarily a standing committee. Taken from the linked shco_kb committee record for the Antimicrobial Stewardship Team (AST), which records this as AccredReady's recommended practice rather than NABH book text.
- The SHCO 3rd Edition book does not specify AST meeting frequency, membership, quorum or chairperson. These are therefore written as "[Hospital to define]" rather than invented.

RECONCILIATION PASS — EXPOSURE FIRST AID AND PEP TIMING (added 2026-08-13)
The first-aid sentence on antiseptics was rewritten and is now byte-identical in the infection prevention and control practices policy and the occupational health and post-exposure policy. Both previously grouped antiseptic with caustic agents and prohibited it outright, which overstated the source and risked contradicting local practice, since povidone-iodine after washing is common in Indian protocols.
SOURCE, verified 2026-08-13 against the guideline itself: US Public Health Service, Updated US Public Health Service Guidelines for the Management of Occupational Exposures to Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Recommendations for Postexposure Prophylaxis (Kuhar et al., 2013). Its position is three-part and the documents now state all three: wounds and skin sites are washed with soap and water and mucous membranes flushed with water; there is no evidence that antiseptics for wound care, or expressing fluid by squeezing the wound, further reduce the risk of transmission; and the application of caustic agents such as bleach, or the injection of antiseptics or disinfectants into the wound, is not recommended. Note the distinction the documents now preserve: injecting antiseptic into the wound is not recommended, whereas applying antiseptic to the site is merely unproven, not prohibited.
PEP TIMING. The first-dose wording is now identical in both documents: as soon as possible, ideally within hours and preferably within two, and not beyond 72 hours.
REVIEWER TO NOTE — THE TWO-HOUR FIGURE IS NOT FROM THE CURRENT GUIDELINE. A 2025 revision exists (2025 US Public Health Service Guidelines for the Management of Occupational Exposures to HIV, Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol). It states "Initiate PEP as soon as possible, up to 72 hours following the occupational exposure to HIV" and carries no "within two hours" figure. The two-hour wording was adopted across both documents on instruction, to remove a divergence between them, and it is not clinically wrong — earlier is better — but it should not be attributed to the 2025 guideline. The 2025 revision also adds a recommendation NEITHER document carries: where an exposure beyond 72 hours is thought to represent a high risk of transmission, consult a provider with expertise in HIV treatment rather than treating 72 hours as an absolute cut-off.
